Learning Outcomes

The ultimate goal of this course is to develop critical thinking skills and habits of mind for evaluating the relationship between primary sources (data), fact, and analytical implications: How do we know what we think we know? What is a fact? Everyone has an opinion: what is the difference between a more compelling and less compelling argument?

This may seem vague, and to some degree this is what all humanities courses purport to do. What about the “hard skills” you can put on your résumé?

Reading Primary Sources

A primary source is a piece of evidence from the past: a chronicle, a decree, a letter, a travel account. Reading one competently means asking who wrote it, for whom, and why; what it can tell us; and, just as important, what it cannot.

The same skill applies to any document you will ever need to evaluate, from a news story to a contract to a viral post: who made this, for whom, and why should I believe it?

Analytical Writing

Reports of the demise of analytical writing are greatly exaggerated: for all the ways AI is reshaping the way we write (see AI in This Course), your ability to draw upon facts to advance an argument-driven interpretation of those facts (in print or out loud; in an academic essay or on social media; to a friend or to your supervisor) is more valuable than ever before.

In this course, you will practice that skill mostly by hand, in class: short responses and mini-essays that ask you to make an argument quickly, clearly, and with evidence, without a safety net (see Writing by Hand in Class).

Arguing Out Loud

Much of the reasoning you will do in your career will happen in conversation: in meetings, interviews, and arguments with people who disagree with you. We will practice this in a structured way: moderated discussions and presentations in this course ask you to state an interpretation, support it with evidence, respond to counterarguments, and disagree productively.

“Knowing Stuff”

Can you name all of the US state capitals, or recite any of Shakespeare’s sonnets? Your parents grandparents probably could, or memorized them in school. As more and more information is at our disposal on our smartphones, less and less of it is readily available in our heads. For the most part, that is as it should be: pedagogy evolves along with our tools.

However… it is still important to have some baseline of knowledge in your active memory. Even though you can look up a fact in a matter of seconds, in practice much of the time you will not do so: when you are chatting on the phone, as you quickly peruse an article, when you don’t know what you don’t know. The facts at your immediate disposal in your active memory shape your understanding of the world around you even when you don’t realize it.

Therefore, you will be expected to learn some stuff — even (gasp) memorize a few big-picture facts — relevant to the subject matter of this course. That is one reason so many evaluations in this course happen in class, by hand (see Grading Policies).

Managing Information

Readings, audio lectures, video lectures, live discussion: this course gives you a lot of information in a lot of formats. Building your own system for capturing and organizing it in a way that will be “legible to your future self” is a skill that will outlast any single course (see Note-Taking).

Judging AI Output

Which came first, the chicken or the egg? Strong writers use AI effectively in part because they first learned to write the old-fashioned way. So how do you learn to ride without training wheels when training wheels are always within reach? Part of the answer is simply to take them off for a while, which is what the handwritten, in-class work in this course is for.

Everything above makes you a better user of AI. Knowing some facts lets you notice when a confident answer is wrong. Reading sources critically lets you notice when evidence has been invented. Writing and arguing for yourself gives you the standards to tell substantive prose from empty prose. AI is most useful to people who could, in a pinch, do without it. For how this course puts that into practice, see AI in This Course.
